steps.step: The receiver works out distance from the travel time: travel time = receive time − the send time stamped by the satellite, and distance = travel time × c.
steps.idea: The satellite's time stamp feeds straight into the travel time, so any error in the satellite clock becomes an error in the travel time.

steps.step: Light travels about 30 cm per nanosecond, so a 10 ns timing error gives a distance error of about 10 × 30 cm = 3 m.
steps.part: Step 1, paragraph 3 ("Light travels about 30 cm per nanosecond")
steps.idea: Each nanosecond of clock error is worth about 30 cm of distance. This matches Step 4's figure of 26 ns ≈ 8 m.

steps.step: Which way the error goes: a fast satellite clock stamps a send time that is too late, so receive − send comes out about 10 ns too short. The distance to that satellite is then about 3 m too short.
steps.part: Step 1 paragraph 2 (travel time = receive − send) plus background arithmetic
steps.idea: Subtracting a send time that is too large gives a travel time that is too small.

steps.step: The receiver's clock bias b adds the same amount, c·b, to every pseudorange. That is why one extra unknown can soak it up when four satellites are used.
steps.part: Step 2: why four satellites, not three (pseudorange equation ρᵢ = √(...) + c·b)
steps.idea: The receiver's clock error is common to all four measurements, and the term for it is identical in every equation.

steps.step: The 10 ns error is in one satellite's clock, so only that one pseudorange is off by about 3 m. The other three are correct. One shared b cannot match an error that appears in a single equation. The solver instead finds a compromise that pulls the position (and b) away from the true values.
steps.part: Step 2 ("plus the same error c·b"); Limits, first bullet ("b absorbs part of an error that all satellites share"); Step 2 paragraph 3 ("This method works only if the satellite clocks all keep GPS time")
steps.idea: b can only absorb an error that is the same for every satellite. An error that belongs to one satellite breaks the model's assumption that all satellite clocks keep GPS time.

result: The distance to that satellite is off by about 3 m (10 ns × about 30 cm/ns). Because the fast clock stamps a send time that is too late, the measured distance comes out about 3 m too short. The receiver's fourth unknown, b, cannot absorb this. b enters every pseudorange as the same term, c·b, so it can only cancel an error that all satellites share, such as the receiver's own clock offset. This 3 m error is in only one of the four equations, so no single value of b fits all four. The solver ends up shifting the position estimate, and b, by a few metres instead. This is why the method needs every satellite clock to keep GPS time.
